name: Nebuchadnezzar
source_summary: King of Babylon who conquered Jerusalem in multiple stages, destroyed the temple, and deported Judah into exile; also the ruler under whom Daniel and his three companions served, whose troubling dreams Daniel interpreted, who cast Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into a fiery furnace, and who was himself humbled with a period of madness until he acknowledged the sovereignty of the Most High.
family_friendly_summary: Nebuchadnezzar was the powerful king of Babylon who conquered the kingdom of Judah and destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, carrying many people, including Daniel and his three friends, off into exile. Even though he was a mighty and often cruel king, God worked in his life in remarkable ways. Nebuchadnezzar had troubling dreams that only Daniel, with God's help, could explain. When Daniel's three friends refused to bow to a giant golden statue, Nebuchadnezzar threw them into a blazing furnace -- but God protected them completely. Later, God humbled the proud king directly, causing him to lose his mind for a time until he learned that 'the Most High is ruler over the realm of mankind.' After this experience, Nebuchadnezzar praised and honored the true God.
adult_story: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon, dominates the biblical narrative of Judah's final decades as an independent kingdom. He besieged Jerusalem multiple times, first making King Jehoiakim his vassal, then deporting King Jehoiachin along with the temple treasures and thousands of Judah's elite when Jehoiachin rebelled (2 Kings 24:1-17), and finally, after King Zedekiah's rebellion, destroying Jerusalem entirely -- burning the temple and palace, breaking down the city walls, and deporting most of the remaining population (2 Kings 25:1-21; 2 Chronicles 36:17-20). Jeremiah repeatedly identifies Nebuchadnezzar's conquest, however brutal, as an instrument of God's judgment on Judah's persistent covenant unfaithfulness, even calling him God's 'servant' in this specific capacity (Jeremiah 25:9; 27:6). Within Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar features prominently in the book of Daniel: he had Daniel and three Judean companions trained for his court (Daniel 1), was troubled by a dream of a great statue that Daniel alone could recall and interpret, revealing a succession of coming kingdoms (Daniel 2), and set up a golden image demanding worship, casting Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego into a furnace when they refused -- only to see them emerge unharmed and to praise their God as a result (Daniel 3). Most strikingly, Daniel 4 records, in Nebuchadnezzar's own voice, a second dream warning of his coming humbling for pride; when the warning went unheeded, he was driven from human society and 'ate grass like cattle' for a period until, at its end, 'I raised my eyes toward heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High... His kingdom endures from generation to generation' (Daniel 4:34) -- Scripture's own record of the proudest king of his age brought low and, at least in this account, brought to acknowledge the true God.
christ_connections: Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great statue in Daniel 2, in which a stone 'cut out without hands' shatters the kingdoms of the world and grows to fill the earth, has long been read by Christian interpreters as pointing to Christ's kingdom, which overturns and outlasts every human empire.

The mysterious 'fourth man' seen walking unharmed with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the furnace, described as like 'a son of the gods' (Daniel 3:25), has traditionally been understood by many readers as a preincarnate appearance of Christ standing with His faithful people -- though Scripture does not name him, so this remains a traditional reading.

Nebuchadnezzar's own humbling and eventual confession that 'the Most High is ruler over the realm of mankind' (Daniel 4:25) testifies, even from a pagan emperor's mouth, to the sovereignty Christ Himself claims fully in the New Testament (Matthew 28:18).
